title: Market Street Errand
story: On Saturdays a long street becomes a market. Stalls stand in one row, each selling one kind of thing, written as a letter: b for bread, h for honey, e for eggs. Several stalls can sell the same thing. Read from one end, the street is a string like "ebxhbqe".
Your shopping list, wanted, is also letters, and each stall sells you one item. Your bags are heavy, so you want the shortest unbroken section of street where you can buy everything.
task: Write shortestErrand(street, wanted). Return the shortest substring of street containing every character of wanted, including repeats. For example, if wanted has two h's, the substring needs at least two. Extra stalls inside the substring are fine.
On a tie for shortest, return the leftmost. If no section works, return "". Letters are case-sensitive.
constraints: street and wanted contain letters a-z and A-Z only.

examples.explanation: ebxh (stalls 0 to 3) has e, b and h, length 4. hbqe (stalls 3 to 6) also has all three at length 4, but starts later. Every 3-stall section misses at least one item.
The list needs two h's and an e. hbhxxe (length 6) works, but hxxeh (stalls 2 to 6, length 5) is shorter. Counting only kinds, not how many, would wrongly accept eh.

hints: In the first example, walk from the start until you have everything, which happens at stall 3 with ebxh. Could you drop the first stall and still have everything? What does that tell you about where to look next?
Every valid section ends at some stall, and for each end you want the latest start that still covers the list. As the end moves right, that best start never moves left.

So use a sliding window. Move the right edge one stall at a time. When the window covers the list, pull the left edge in as far as it stays covering, record it, and then pull once more to break it and continue.

To check "covers the list" in O(1), keep need (how many of each letter the list still wants) and missing (how many list items are uncovered). When a stall enters and need[c] > 0, decrease missing; decrease need[c] either way. When missing is 0, shrink from the left, adding back to need and increasing missing when it goes above 0. Record a window only if strictly shorter, which keeps the leftmost tie.
bruteForce: Try every start and end, count the letters, and check them against the list. Or try each length from 1 upward and stop at the first that works.
A 10,000-stall street has about 50 million sections, each costly to check. Even the smarter version recounts overlapping sections, though neighbours differ by just one stall.

js: * @param {string} wanted  items to buy, repeats allowed
* @return {string} shortest covering section, leftmost on ties, or ""

walkthrough: Slide a window over the street. The right edge adds stalls until the window covers the list. Then the left edge removes stalls for as long as the window still covers the list, and each removal gives a shorter candidate. Once the window stops covering the list, the right edge grows again.

The bookkeeping uses two values. need[c] is how many more c's the window wants (a negative value means spares), and missing is the total still wanted. The window covers the list exactly when missing is 0.
Trace "ebxhbqe" with list "hbe" (need h 1, b 1, e 1, missing 3):
• Adding e (stall 0) makes missing 2, adding b makes it 1, and adding x leaves it unchanged because x is not wanted (need[x] = -1).
• Adding h (stall 3) makes missing 0, so the best so far is ebxh with length 4. Dropping e puts need[e] back to 1 and missing back to 1, so shrinking stops.
• Adding b (stall 4) is a spare because need[b] was 0, so missing stays 1, and adding q is also a spare.

• Adding e (stall 6) makes missing 0 with the window bxhbqe, length 6, which is not better. Dropping the spare b gives xhbqe, length 5, and dropping x gives hbqe, length 4, which ties and is not strictly shorter, so the leftmost answer stays. Dropping h makes missing 1, so shrinking stops.
The answer is ebxh. Each stall is added once and dropped at most once, so the work is linear.
solution.timeWhy: Counting the list is O(m). Each stall enters and leaves the window at most once.
solution.spaceWhy: The need map has at most 52 letters.
solution.takeaway: For "shortest window containing everything", track what is still missing with one counter so checking the window is O(1). Grow the window until nothing is missing, shrink it while nothing is missing, and record the best window inside the shrinking loop.
